text: Every log source this chapter has covered — syslog, Windows Event Forwarding, agent- or agentless-collected data — arrives at the SIEM as raw text. Log parsing is the process of extracting structured fields — source IP, username, timestamp, event type — out of that text, so each piece becomes something the SIEM can actually filter, sort, and compare on, instead of just stored characters nobody can query directly.

Take the syslog line from Lesson 9 again: a failed SSH password attempt against user admin from a specific source IP and port. To a human the meaning is obvious. To a SIEM, it's still just an unstructured string until a parser — typically a regular expression, or a known schema like CEF's key-value pairs — runs against it and extracts the pieces that matter.

After parsing, that same line becomes named fields: severity, process, event type, destination user, source IP, source port. Now an analyst can search event_type equals Failed Logon and dest_user equals admin and get every matching event across the entire log volume instantly, instead of scanning raw text line by line looking for the right pattern.

This matters beyond search. Chapter 4's correlation rules compare field values across different log sources — flagging when the same source IP shows up in a failed logon and then a successful one minutes later. Different sources often name the same concept differently: src_ip, SourceAddress, sourceIPAddress. Normalization maps all of those into one shared field name, often against a published schema like Splunk's Common Information Model or Microsoft Sentinel's Advanced Security Information Model, so every rule and dashboard can rely on one consistent name.

Without normalization, a rule written against src_ip would quietly miss events logged under a different field name from another source — exactly the kind of gap that matters in a real investigation, not just a cosmetic inconsistency. Next, Chapter 4 opens with what a correlation rule actually is, built entirely on the parsed, normalized fields this lesson covered.
